prompt: All winter, a tea brand's ads show its logo beside a crackling fireplace. Match each part of classical conditioning to what happens in the campaign.

pairs.match: The sound of a crackling fire in every ad
pairs.explanation: The crackling fire is the unconditioned stimulus: like upbeat music, it naturally triggers positive feelings.

pairs.match: Feeling warm and cozy whenever a fire crackles
pairs.explanation: The cozy feeling is the natural response the fire brings, before any learning has happened.

pairs.match: The tea logo, before anyone has seen the ads
pairs.explanation: At first the logo brings no feeling at all, so it is the neutral stimulus.

pairs.match: Ad after ad showing the logo right beside the fire
pairs.explanation: The brand pairs the fire with its logo repeatedly, so the two become linked.

pairs.match: Feeling cozy on seeing the logo alone on a shelf
pairs.explanation: Seeing the brand alone now produces the positive feeling. This is a conditioned response.

prompt: Each case below shows repetition at work, or a learned response spreading or narrowing. Name what is happening.

cases.text: A new gym plays the same short jingle on the radio every morning for a month. By the end, listeners hum it when they pass the gym.
cases.explanation: Repetition: repeated exposures strengthen the link between the jingle and the gym.

cases.text: The same insurance ad plays in every video break for weeks. Viewers start muting it the moment it begins.
cases.explanation: Advertising wear-out: too much repetition makes consumers tune out or get annoyed.

cases.text: A pharmacy sells its own pain relievers in the same blue-and-yellow box as the best-selling brand, and shoppers trust them straight away.
cases.explanation: Stimulus generalization: a similar-looking box triggers the trust shoppers learned for the leader.

cases.text: A sneaker brand's ads keep showing close-ups of its one-of-a-kind stitched heel, so buyers can tell its shoes from copies.
cases.explanation: Stimulus discrimination: the brand teaches consumers to spot the unique difference between products.

cases.text: A candy brand keeps short ads running all year so shoppers do not lose the link between its logo and fun.
cases.explanation: Repetition: repeated exposures prevent memory decay and keep the link strong.

cases.text: A toy maker gives its new board game the same lettering and colours as a famous game. Children get as excited as they do for the famous one.
cases.explanation: Stimulus generalization: similar stimuli trigger the same learned response.

cases.text: A fast-food jingle plays in every radio break for months, until listeners roll their eyes and switch stations.
cases.explanation: Advertising wear-out: too much repetition makes consumers tune out or get annoyed.

cases.text: A butter brand prints a gold seal on every pack and runs ads saying 'only the real one has the seal.' Shoppers now check for it.
cases.explanation: Stimulus discrimination: the brand teaches consumers to spot what makes it different from look-alikes.

prompt: Lena watches a fitness coach online; Sami watches a star striker. Sort each moment into the step of observational learning it belongs to.

cards.text: Lena stops scrolling to watch a trusted fitness coach's morning video.
cards.explanation: First, the consumer directs attention to an attractive or credible model.

cards.text: Sami watches the star striker's boots for the whole match.
cards.explanation: First, the consumer directs attention to an attractive model.

cards.text: Days later, Lena can still describe the blender the coach used.
cards.explanation: Second, the consumer remembers what the model says or does.

cards.text: At the mall, Sami recalls the exact colour of the striker's boots.
cards.explanation: Second, the consumer remembers what the model says or does.

cards.text: Lena orders the same blender online.
cards.explanation: Third, the consumer converts the memory into action by purchasing the same product.

cards.text: Sami saves his allowance and buys the same boots.
cards.explanation: Third, the consumer converts the memory into action by purchasing the same product.

prompt: Each case below shows a brand message in one of the three memory stores. Name the store at work.

cases.text: Walking past a bakery, you glimpse a poster in the window. A few seconds later it is gone from your mind.
cases.explanation: Sensory memory holds brief sensory inputs for a few seconds. This poster never got your attention.

cases.text: A radio host reads out a promo code, and you repeat it to yourself while you look for a pen.
cases.explanation: Short-term memory holds a small amount of information in active consciousness for about twenty seconds.

cases.text: You can still sing the jingle from a cereal ad you loved as a child.
cases.explanation: Long-term memory retains information for days, months, or years.

cases.text: From a car window, a billboard flashes past. Only its red colour registers for a moment.
cases.explanation: Sensory memory holds brief sensory inputs for a few seconds before they fade.

cases.text: A pizza ad reads its number as "514 · 555 · 0199", so you can hold it in mind while you dial.
cases.explanation: Chunking helps short-term memory: three chunks fit where ten separate digits would not.

cases.text: A runner thinks through how a new running app fits her training plan. Months later she still knows the brand well.
cases.explanation: Elaborative rehearsal moved the brand into long-term memory, which lasts for days, months, or years.
